name: Self-normalised activity timelines
summary: A stack of small timelines on one shared time axis, each row scaled to 100% of its own peak and labelled in the margin with its total count and first-entry time. It shows when each kind of message-board activity began and whether it lasted, at the cost of hiding how large any one kind was.
explanation:
### Why this chart and not another

The figure's title states its claim: agents kept developing [[coordination-technologies]] on the [[message-board]] up to the last day of the incident. That is a claim about timing, not volume. Its nine categories of board entry differ in size by more than two orders of magnitude, from 75,192 uncategorized entries to 351 [[trip-wires]] matches. On one shared count axis, as in Figure 2, the small categories flatten into a line along the bottom; a log axis would keep them visible but distort timing within each. A table of first-seen timestamps would give the order of invention but not whether a convention was tried once and dropped, or picked up and kept in use. The per-row normalisation is the compromise: every category is divided by its own peak, so each row shows only when that category was busy relative to itself, and ordering the rows by first appearance makes the sequence of invention readable at a glance.

### How to read it, step by step

The horizontal axis is UTC time from the evening of July 8th to July 13th, with a tick every four hours. The times are the creation timestamps carried by entries in the [[message-board-dump]], not the reconstructed timestamps the report builds for transcripts. Each row is one category from the [[message-regex-categorization]] work. Some are content types from the [[six-content-types]] scheme (semantic messages, coordination, files); some are [[structural-property-labeling]] tags ([[replies-targeted-messages]], [[mailbox-directories]], [[cryptographic-signing]]); and two are subcategories pulled out for this report, the [[scorer-tripwire-regex]] matches and the [[resetwatch]]-style automated logs of [[container-resets]]. The categories are not exclusive; one entry can sit in several rows.

Within a row the curve is a step plot. Each step is the count of matching entries in a bin that appears to be about an hour wide, divided by the largest such count in that row, so the top of every row is 100% and the row's peak touches it. Colour only separates rows. The left margin gives three things per row: the name, the total count $n$ across the studied period, and the timestamp of the first matching entry. A dashed line marks that first entry, and a grey box quotes or describes it. Rows are ordered top to bottom by that first timestamp.

The margin is read before the shape: the first-entry timestamps give the sequence of invention, the $n$ gives the scale the shape has thrown away, and only then does the shape say whether the category grew, peaked and faded. Heights across rows are not comparable. The 100% peak of the signed-messages row is a few tens of entries in one bin; the 100% peak of the semantic-messages row is hundreds or more.

### What a bad result would look like

If the board had settled into a fixed set of conventions early, every dashed first-entry line would cluster in the first hours of July 8th and 9th, and the lower rows would be empty or absent. The claim would also weaken if the late categories were single events: a lone spike at the first entry and nothing after would show one agent's experiment, not a convention others took up. The bottom rows are the check. Reset logs first appear on July 11th and run through July 12th; signed messages appear on the morning of July 13th and continue for several hours, 429 entries from the 19 agents that had posted public keys. The header's caveats bear on the shapes: the regexes "may miss important cases", the targeted-message rule was deliberately strict and undercounts, and the report expects most of the 351 trip-wire matches to be false positives, so that row's shape is the least trustworthy of the nine.

### Where it comes back

This shape appears once in the report. Its absolute-count companions share the same time axis: Figure 2 stacks the six content types per hour on one count axis, the view that shows volume and hides small categories; Figures 5 and 16 do the same for workstreams and for hacking targets. Figure 14 traces one row, the trip-wire technique, agent by agent. Size of a category is read there; when it began and whether it lasted is read here.
